title_en: Homily on “I Am Going to My Father”
author: Cyril of Jerusalem
occasion: The homily explains the saying of Christ, “I am going to my Father; and whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” It addresses how the same “I” can be used of both Christ’s divinity and his humanity.
argument: Cyril explains that when Christ says “I am going to my Father,” the pronoun “I” is used of both the divine and the human natures. The meaning of the words is shown by their context, while the distinction of the natures is shown by the difference in what is said. Because Christ speaks in both cases as of one person, the text signifies the union of the person. The homily thus expounds the unity of Christ’s person while distinguishing his two natures.

outline.move: Cyril introduces the Gospel saying and explains that the same “I” is used of Christ’s divinity and humanity, showing the union of his person while distinguishing the natures.

cast.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
cast.who: Bishop of Jerusalem and the author of the homily.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The speaker of the Gospel saying, whose person unites divinity and humanity; referred to in the text by the pronoun “I” (τὸ ἐγώ).

key_terms.sense: The pronoun “I” used by Christ of himself
The union or joining of Christ’s person

scripture: The homily quotes John 14:12b–13 in a form close to the Greek Gospel text. Psalm numbering and Old Testament book names are not used in the surviving text.

Whether the homily originally continued beyond the surviving fragment

_unresolved_facts.claim: The meaning of the words is shown by their context, while the distinction of the natures is shown by the difference in what is said.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς τὴν μὲν διάνοιαν τῶν ῥημάτων ἐκ τῆς ἀκολουθίας φαίνεσθαι, τὴν δὲ διάγνωσιν τῶν φύσεων ἐκ τῆς διαφορᾶς τῶν λεγομένων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The meaning of the words (διάνοια τῶν ῥημάτων) is shown by their sequence/connection (ἀκολουθία), while the discernment/diagnosis of the natures (διάγνωσις τῶν φύσεων) is shown by the difference in what is said.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Because Christ speaks in both cases as of one person, the text signifies the union of the person.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐκ δὲ τοῦ διαλέγεσθαι ἐν ἀμφοτέραις ὡσὰν περὶ ἑνός τινος τὴν τοῦ προσώπου συνάφειαν σημαίνει
_unresolved_facts.fix: Because he converses in both as if about one, he signifies the connection/union of the person. Note: the subject is the text/Christ speaking, but 'συνάφεια' (connection, conjunction) is more technical than 'union' in later Chalcedonian usage.

The Gospel saying appears in the title/incipit as a lemma, not as a direct quotation marked within Cyril's discourse. The brief should note this is a lemmatic citation in the title, not a voice marked within the homily body.

_unresolved_facts.claim: referred to in the text by the pronoun "I" (τὸ ἐγώ)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Christ is referred to by the pronoun 'I' (ἐγώ) in the Gospel saying itself; the homily discusses how this 'I' (τὸ ἐγώ) is placed/used (τίθησιν) with reference to both natures.
